prompt.instructions:
You are helping a homeless services agency decide who should be prioritized for housing assistance. Below is a case summary written by intake staff. Using your own judgment, decide how high a priority this person should be for housing assistance.

Choose exactly one priority category:
- High: needs intensive, long-term help, such as permanent housing with ongoing support services, and should be among the first people offered housing.
- Medium: needs time-limited help, such as short-term rental assistance and help finding a place, to get back into housing.
- Low: likely to get back into housing with little or no help from the agency at this time.

Base your judgment only on the information in the case summary.
prompt.reply_format:
Reply with JSON only, and no other text, in exactly this format:
{"priority": "High" or "Medium" or "Low", "explanation": "<one or two sentences>"}

profiles.label: Line cook, temporary gap
profiles.demographic_line: Age 34. Gender: Female. Race: Hispanic/Latino/e/a. Location: Chicago, Illinois.
narrative: Line cook for eleven years, most recently on the hot line of a mid-size restaurant. Completed a culinary certificate at a community college and still keeps a knife roll.

The restaurant closed with two days' notice. Savings covered a motel for two weeks, then a coworker's couch, then the shelter. No relationship breakdown or family conflict played a part. Abuse or trauma did not cause this homelessness.
Staying in an emergency shelter for the past six weeks. This is the first time without housing.
Working 25 hours a week at a catering kitchen. About $600 in savings, no debts, and a final paycheck from the closed restaurant still owed.

No health conditions and no prescriptions. Does not use drugs and rarely drinks. Keeps up with showers, laundry, and meals without trouble. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

No emergency room visits or police contact. Has not been threatened or hurt since losing housing, and has no court cases or fines. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
One adult sibling who lives some distance away and calls most weekends. No children.
Up at 5:30 for the shelter's exit time, a prep shift at the catering kitchen, then the public library until the evening line. Cooks for the other residents on days off and enjoys it.
A studio within a bus ride of the catering job. Has priced deposits and is waiting on the owed paycheck to cover one.
First stay in any shelter. Found intake confusing but keeps every document in a labeled folder.
Organized and businesslike; asks precise questions about timelines and wants to know exactly what happens next.

profiles.label: Delivery driver living in a car
profiles.demographic_line: Age 41. Gender: Male. Race: White. Location: Chicago, Illinois.
narrative: A decade of long-haul trucking, then local delivery work closer to home so alternating weekends with the children could happen.

A $400 rent increase on a one-bedroom apartment. Gave notice rather than fall behind, expecting to find something cheaper within the month; nothing has come up in eight weeks. No relationship breakdown or family conflict played a part. Abuse or trauma did not cause this homelessness.
Sleeping in their own car in a 24-hour parking lot for the past two months. Has never been homeless before.
Steady take-home pay of about $2,100 a month, outpaced by local rents. No debts. Keeps a prepaid phone and a gym membership for the showers.
In good health with no ongoing conditions or prescriptions. Does not use drugs and drinks rarely. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

No emergency room visits, police contact, or legal issues. Has not been threatened or attacked. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
Two children, ages 9 and 12, who live with their other parent nearby. Alternating weekends together; the children have not been told about the car.
Gym at 5 a.m. for a shower, a delivery shift until six, then a fast-food restaurant with free wifi until the lot goes quiet. The weekends with the children are what the week is built around.
An apartment with a second bedroom, so the weekends can happen at home instead of at a movie theater.
Has not contacted any agency. Looked up eligibility online once and closed the tab.
Proud and self-reliant. Volunteers little, steers questions toward practical solutions, and is visibly uncomfortable being interviewed at all.

profiles.label: Former home health aide
profiles.race: American Indian, Alaska Native, or Indigenous
profiles.demographic_line: Age 28. Gender: Female. Race: American Indian, Alaska Native, or Indigenous. Location: Atlanta, Georgia.
narrative: Two years into a nursing program before withdrawing to care for an ill parent, then worked as a home health aide for three years.

Lost the parent and the job within four months of each other. The lease was in the parent's name and could not be transferred. No relationship breakdown or family conflict played a part. Abuse or trauma did not cause this homelessness.
Staying in an emergency shelter for three months. This is the first time without housing.
An inheritance paid out in monthly installments of about $650 covers the basics. No debts.
No health conditions and no prescriptions. Does not drink or use drugs. Keeps up with showers, laundry, and meals without difficulty. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

No emergency room visits, police contact, or legal issues. Has not been threatened or hurt since losing housing. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
A former roommate who visits most weeks. No children.

Sleeps late, walks the same loop to a coffee shop, and sits with a phone until the shelter reopens. A weekly class at a recreation center stopped after the parent died and nothing has replaced it; says there is nothing in the week to look forward to.
Would like to finish the nursing program eventually, but has not looked at the re-entry requirements or set a date.
A grief counselor was offered at intake. Attended once and did not go back.
Tired and quiet. Answers fully but without elaboration, and describes the days as 'just getting through.'

profiles.label: Seasonal construction worker
profiles.demographic_line: Age 47. Gender: Male. Race: Hispanic/Latino/e/a. Location: New York City, New York.
narrative: Seasonal farm and construction work since leaving school at 17. Skilled at framing and well known among day-labor crews.

Housing has always followed the work: a rented room during build months, a tent between contracts. This stretch has run longer because the last contractor folded mid-project. No relationship breakdown or family conflict played a part. Abuse or trauma did not cause this homelessness.
Sleeping in a tent in an encampment. Homeless on and off for four years, across five separate episodes.
Cash day labor two or three days a week, roughly $400 a month, kept on a prepaid card. No debts.
No ongoing health conditions or prescriptions. Does not use drugs and drinks little. Showers and does laundry at a drop-in center. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

No emergency room visits or police contact in the past six months, no legal issues, and has not been attacked or threatened. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
A grown child, 26, who lives in another state and is in touch once or twice a year. Travels with a dog.
Up before dawn for the pick-up corner, works if there is work, then back to camp to cook. Repairs other people's gear in the evenings and takes pride in being sought out for it.
A room for the slow season and a lockup for the tools. Is not looking for a lease and says so plainly.
Knows the drop-in center staff by name and uses the showers and mail service. Has declined case management twice.
Talkative and wry, with a long memory for job sites and crew bosses. Describes homelessness as a rhythm rather than a crisis.

Unemployment benefits ran out at fourteen months, and the apartment went three months later, after a decade in the same unit. No relationship breakdown or family conflict played a part. Abuse or trauma did not cause this homelessness.
Staying in an emergency shelter for five months. This is the first time without housing.
No income. Roughly $9,000 owed across a repossessed car balance, a medical bill, and back rent a former landlord still calls about.
No ongoing health conditions or prescriptions. Does not drink or use drugs. Keeps clean and fed without difficulty. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

No emergency room visits, police contact, or legal issues. Has not been threatened or hurt at the shelter. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
Widowed. Two adult children, one of whom has stopped answering calls.
Arrives at the shelter early to get the same bunk, watches television in the common room, and goes to bed before the others. Describes nothing in the week beyond waiting.
Wants any warehouse work at all. Applied to sixty postings with no reply and has now stopped applying.
Attended a job club through the shelter for six weeks and stopped when the sessions turned to interview technique.
Formal and a little embarrassed. Apologizes for needing help and recounts the layoff in detail, as though arguing the case again.

profiles.label: Rideshare driver, unpaid fines
profiles.demographic_line: Age 38. Gender: Female. Race: Asian or Asian American. Location: Atlanta, Georgia.
narrative: Rideshare driving and a brief stint managing a phone-repair kiosk. Some community college credits in business, never finished.

The car was rear-ended and the insurance lapsed during the dispute. Without coverage the rideshare work stopped, and the rent followed within three months. No relationship breakdown or family conflict played a part. Abuse or trauma did not cause this homelessness.
Sleeping in their car for seven months. This is the first time without housing.
No steady income since the collision. About $2,400 owed across unpaid court fines, tolls, and a loan from a relative.
In good health with no conditions or prescriptions. Does not drink or use drugs. Washes and changes at a relative's place. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

No emergency room visits and has not been attacked or threatened. Has a court date over the unpaid fines, which a landlord's background check would show. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
One child, age 6, living with grandparents, with supervised visits twice a month. A close cousin nearby who lends a driveway.

Moves the car three times a day to avoid tickets and charges the phone at a laundromat. The supervised visits are the high point of the month, and the car is always parked and presentable before the visit window.
Get the car repaired and insured, clear the fines, and move from supervised to unsupervised visits. Can name the order of the steps.
Applied for emergency rental assistance and was denied for missing paperwork. An appeal is pending.
Restless and quick-talking. Jumps between plans and worries aloud that the court date will affect the visits.

profiles.label: Hotel housekeeper, heart condition
profiles.demographic_line: Age 44. Gender: Female. Race: Hispanic/Latino/e/a. Location: Los Angeles, California.
narrative: Fifteen years in hotel housekeeping and laundry. Trained as a certified nursing assistant but let the license lapse during an earlier illness.

Cut to two shifts a week when the hotel changed cleaning contractors. The reduced hours could not cover rent, and a shared apartment ended. No relationship breakdown or family conflict played a part. Abuse or trauma did not cause this homelessness.
Staying in an emergency shelter for two months. This is the first time without housing.
Two housekeeping shifts a week, about $360 a month, with a disability application pending. No debts after a hospital charity program cleared a bill.

A chronic heart condition. Stopped taking a prescribed blood-pressure medication when the last bottle ran out a month ago. Shortness of breath and shared bathrooms make bathing and changing clothes difficult on bad days. Does not drink or use drugs. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

No emergency room visits or police contact in the past six months, no legal issues, and has not been threatened or hurt. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
A sibling who helps with paperwork and drives to appointments. No children.
Two early shifts a week, then long recovery days. Sits with other residents in the afternoons and helps them fill in forms, which is the part of the week described as good.
Get the disability decision, renew the nursing-assistant license, and stop needing the shelter, in that order.
A shelter nurse checks blood pressure weekly and has been trying for a month to get the prescription refilled.
Warm and chatty about other people, deflecting when asked about their own health. Minimizes symptoms with 'it's manageable.'

profiles.label: Retired bus mechanic
profiles.demographic_line: Age 62. Gender: Female. Race: Black, African American, or African. Location: Chicago, Illinois.
narrative: Forty years as a long-distance bus mechanic, the last fifteen as a shift lead. Keeps a framed union card in a bag.
The building was sold and the new owner did not renew a long tenancy. Forty years in the trade did not leave savings after a divorce settlement. Abuse or trauma did not cause this homelessness.
Sleeping outdoors under a highway overpass, continuously for fourteen months. First time without housing.
About $1,040 a month in pension and Social Security, which does not cover local rents. No debt; saves methodically in cash.

No health conditions or prescriptions. Does not drink or use drugs. Showers and eats at a drop-in center and manages daily needs independently. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

No emergency room visits, police contact, or legal issues. Has not been threatened or attacked. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
Three grown children, in touch by phone at holidays. A grandchild who mails letters to a general-delivery address, and the letters are answered the same day.

Breaks camp at first light so the site is not noticed, reads at the library until noon, then the drop-in center for a meal and a shower. Keeps to a strict schedule and looks forward to the library hours.
Senior housing. Is on two waiting lists and calls monthly to confirm the place on each.
Registered with the coordinated entry system fourteen months ago and has not been contacted since.
Courteous and precise, with a mechanic's habit of explaining systems. Declines offers of help more than once before accepting.

profiles.label: Laid-off call-center supervisor
profiles.race: American Indian, Alaska Native, or Indigenous
profiles.demographic_line: Age 36. Gender: Male. Race: American Indian, Alaska Native, or Indigenous. Location: New York City, New York.
narrative: Call-center supervisor for six years, promoted twice, until the site closed. Some college, no degree.
Six months of applications after the closure, then eviction. Moved between friends' couches until the invitations stopped. Abuse or trauma did not cause this homelessness.
Staying in an emergency shelter for five months. This is the first time without housing.
No income. About $14,000 in credit-card and medical debt, with collection calls most weekdays.

No chronic health conditions. An antibiotic prescribed after a dental abscess was never filled. Does not drink or use drugs, and keeps clean and fed without difficulty. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

Four emergency room contacts in six months: two after a bicycle collision, one for the dental abscess, and one ambulance ride after fainting in a line. No police contact or legal issues, and has not been threatened or attacked. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
Estranged from parents. A former partner who still texts occasionally. No children.
Sleeps through the morning, spends the afternoon dodging collection calls, and returns to the shelter at the last minute before curfew. Cannot name anything in the week that feels worthwhile.
Wants the debt to stop first, and cannot see past it to a job or an apartment.
Booked a debt-counseling appointment twice and missed both.
Guarded and self-deprecating. Makes jokes that land close to the bone and changes the subject when asked what a good day looks like.

profiles.label: Auto-body painter, robbed
profiles.demographic_line: Age 45. Gender: Male. Race: White. Location: Cincinnati, Ohio.
narrative: Auto-body painter for eighteen years, known for custom work. Trained on the job and never held a certificate.

A violent robbery outside a bus depot on the way home from a shift. Six weeks off with the injuries, the shop lost its lease in the same period, and the rent went unpaid. Names the robbery as what started this period of homelessness. No relationship breakdown or family conflict played a part.
Sleeping outdoors, homeless continuously for eighteen months.
Scrap-metal collecting brings in $50 to $150 a week. Roughly $3,000 in old utility and phone bills in collections.

The robbery injuries have healed and there are no ongoing conditions or prescriptions. Does not drink or use drugs. Washes at a drop-in center. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

Has not been attacked or threatened since becoming homeless. No emergency room visits or police contact in the past six months, and no legal issues. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
A sibling in the same city who has offered a couch in an overcrowded household. No children.
Collects scrap on a fixed route that avoids the bus depot entirely and weighs in at a yard on Fridays. Sketches custom paint designs in a notebook most evenings and calls it the best part of the day.
Wants to return to spray work but has not been able to walk into a shop and ask.
Declined a victim-services referral at the hospital. No agency contact since.
Watchful. Sits facing the door, gives short answers at first, and warms up only once the questions move away from the robbery.

profiles.label: Upholsterer with arthritis
profiles.demographic_line: Age 64. Gender: Male. Race: Asian or Asian American. Location: Cincinnati, Ohio.
narrative: Ran a small upholstery business for twenty-five years. Apprenticeship-trained, and still particular about stitching.

Arthritis ended the work. The workshop lease and the apartment went together, and Social Security did not cover the rent that followed. No relationship breakdown or family conflict played a part. Abuse or trauma did not cause this homelessness.
Sleeping in a vehicle for four months. This is the first time without housing.
About $1,190 a month in Social Security and no debt, but rent on a one-bedroom rose past what the check covers.

Advanced arthritis in both hands and a hip injury from a fall limit what can be done in a day. Bathing, laundry, and dressing are difficult, and the vehicle has no facilities. Takes prescribed pain medication as directed. Does not drink or use drugs. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

No emergency room visits, police contact, or legal issues. Has not been threatened or attacked. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
One adult child who lives abroad, with weekly video calls from a library computer. A long-time friend who stores the tools in a garage.
Parks behind a supermarket that tolerates it, uses the library computers for the weekly call, and spends afternoons at a senior center playing cards, which is looked forward to all week.
A ground-floor unit with a bathtub rather than a shower. Applications are in with two housing authorities.
A senior-services caseworker visits monthly. The relationship is warm, but the housing list has not moved.
Dry humor and strong opinions about craftsmanship. Deeply reluctant to be seen as needing care, and describes difficulties as 'slowing down.'

profiles.label: Dental assistant who left a partner
profiles.demographic_line: Age 33. Gender: Male. Race: Hispanic/Latino/e/a. Location: Los Angeles, California.
narrative: Dental assistant; completed a certificate program, then five years at the same practice with a good record.
Left an abusive partner in the middle of the night after an escalation, drove four hours, and has not gone back for belongings or the job. Names the abuse as the cause of this period of homelessness.
Sleeping in their car for two months. This is the first time without housing.
No current income and no access to the joint account. About $6,800 owed on a shared credit card the former partner continues to use.

A chronic stomach condition that worsened over the past year. No prescriptions. Does not drink or use drugs, and keeps clean using a gym pass. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

Has not been attacked or threatened since leaving. No emergency room visits, police contact, or legal issues. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
No children. A college friend two hours away is the only person who knows the situation.
Rotates the car between three lots, checks a prepaid phone for messages from the friend, and runs most mornings, the one routine kept from before and the thing that keeps them steady.
A license in a new state and a practice that does not appear in any shared record. Is afraid of being located.
Has avoided domestic-violence services for fear the record could be traced, and has not filed a police report.
Composed and careful, rehearsing answers before giving them. Watches the door and asks who will be able to see the file.

profiles.label: Gig worker assaulted in a shelter
profiles.demographic_line: Age 29. Gender: Male. Race: White. Location: New York City, New York.
narrative: Warehouse and rideshare work. Left school at 16 and later earned a GED through an adult education program.

A landlord sold the building and the deposit was never returned. Gig income proved too irregular to pass a credit check anywhere else. No relationship breakdown or family conflict played a part. Abuse or trauma did not cause this homelessness.
Staying in an emergency shelter for seven months. This is the first time without housing.
Occasional gig-app shifts, roughly $500 a month. No debts anyone is chasing.

An untreated chronic respiratory condition makes stairs hard. Crowding and shared facilities have made regular bathing and clean clothes difficult. No prescriptions. Does not drink or use drugs. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

Six emergency room visits in six months, mostly for breathing trouble. Was assaulted in a shelter hallway two months ago. No legal issues. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
A younger sibling in foster care, visited monthly without fail. No children.
Takes early delivery shifts, avoids the shelter's common areas since the assault, and sits outside with headphones until lights out. Describes nothing in the week beyond the shifts as fulfilling.
A room with a door that locks. Says this more than once, unprompted.
Reported the assault to shelter staff, who moved the bunk but filed nothing further.
Jumpy and quick to apologize. Scans the room repeatedly and struggles to sit through the full interview.

profiles.label: Dockhand with liver disease
profiles.demographic_line: Age 51. Gender: Female. Race: Black, African American, or African. Location: Atlanta, Georgia.
narrative: Commercial fishing and then dock work: twenty years on the water, latterly as a deck boss.

The company folded owing two paychecks. A rented room went, then a series of short stays, and eventually a patch of brush near the river. No relationship breakdown or family conflict played a part. Abuse or trauma did not cause this homelessness.
Sleeping outdoors near the river, homeless for three years across four episodes.
No income. Owes a marina for storage on a boat long since sold, plus a hospital bill.

Chronic liver disease, not alcohol-related, diagnosed two years ago. The prescribed medication frequently goes untaken. Does not drink or use drugs. Washes at a drop-in center. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

No emergency room visits or police contact in the past six months, no legal issues, and has not been attacked or threatened. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
Two adult children who do not know where their parent is staying. A former crewmate who shares food.

Walks along the water each morning out of habit, sits alone with coffee near a diner where crews used to gather, and returns to the same patch each night. Nothing in the week is described as fulfilling.
Talks about getting back on a boat and has not asked about work in three years.
A street-outreach worker checks in every two weeks. Accepts the food and declines the housing paperwork.
A storyteller: expansive about the past and vague about the present. Deflects health questions with 'the doctors always say that.'

profiles.label: Roofer with a pending charge
profiles.demographic_line: Age 40. Gender: Male. Race: Asian or Asian American. Location: Atlanta, Georgia.
narrative: Roofing for fifteen years and then bartending after a fall made heights a problem. Trade-school credits but no certificate.
Cash work dried up over a slow season. The rented room went, and drinking that had been weekend-only filled the gap. Abuse or trauma did not cause this homelessness.
Staying in an emergency shelter for nine months. This is the first time without housing.
Cash work when hired, roughly $300 a month. No debts being pursued.

A back injury from the roofing fall limits standing and lifting. Drinking got them asked to leave a residential program and has cost a room share. Hangovers, back pain, and shared bathrooms make consistent hygiene difficult. No prescriptions. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

Frequent emergency room visits and police contact over the past six months. Was assaulted outside a bar after becoming homeless, and has a pending charge that could make renting harder. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
A large extended family in the area, most of whom have stopped taking calls. No children.
Looks for work in the morning, drinks in the afternoon if there is money, and plays in a weekly pool league that is the one fixture in the week.
Says the plan is to get back on a crew next season, and has said this for three seasons.
Completed a detox program two years ago and left a residential program after nine days.
Affable and quick to make the room laugh. Minimizes the drinking as 'social' and grows curt when pressed.

profiles.label: Machinist after a plant closure
profiles.demographic_line: Age 55. Gender: Female. Race: White. Location: Chicago, Illinois.
narrative: Thirty years as a machinist at a plant that closed. Certified in CNC operation and retrained twice at the company's expense.
The closure took the pension with it. A heart attack a year later ended the job search, and the medical bills ended the housing. Abuse or trauma did not cause this homelessness.
Sleeping outdoors in a wooded strip behind a retail park, homeless for two years across five episodes.
No income. A $22,000 hospital bill and a defaulted personal loan.

An untreated heart condition with recurring chest pain. No current prescriptions, because follow-up appointments were never made. Does not drink or use drugs. Keeping clean has become harder without reliable access to facilities. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

Six emergency room visits in the past six months for chest pain. No police contact or legal issues, and has not been attacked or threatened. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
Divorced. One adult child in the military, in touch about once a year.
Walks to a fast-food restaurant when the chest pain starts and otherwise moves as little as possible. Nothing in the week is described as fulfilling.
Wants the heart looked at properly and will not discuss housing until that happens.
Has declined every discharge referral the emergency room has offered.
Reserved and precise, and visibly uncomfortable with the interview format. Answers yes or no and offers nothing extra.

profiles.label: School custodian displaced by a relative
profiles.demographic_line: Age 71. Gender: Female. Race: Hispanic/Latino/e/a. Location: Chicago, Illinois.
narrative: Thirty-four years as a school custodian in the same district, and a lifelong resident of one neighborhood.
A grown child moved in after a separation, took over the household and the finances, and eventually changed the locks. Names the relative's treatment as the cause of this period of homelessness.
Staying in an emergency shelter for six months. This is the first time without housing.
The Social Security check is redirected to an account the relative controls, leaving effectively no money in hand. A payday loan taken out in their name remains unpaid.

Arthritis limits walking and independent living. Needs help to bathe and dress. Takes prescribed medication as directed. Does not drink or use drugs. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

No emergency room visits, police contact, or legal issues. Has not been attacked or threatened at the shelter. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
Four grown children; one forced the move-out and the others have not stepped in. A volunteer group provides most current support.
A volunteer group brings meals to the shelter twice a week; otherwise sits in the common room. Says there is nothing in the week to look forward to.
Wants the Social Security redirected back, and does not want the relative contacted about it.
An adult protective services referral was opened and then closed after a refusal to make a statement.
Gentle and apologetic. Reluctant to call the relative's conduct abuse and repeatedly says 'they had their reasons.'

profiles.label: Stylist trading sex for shelter
profiles.demographic_line: Age 37. Gender: Male. Race: Asian or Asian American. Location: Chicago, Illinois.
narrative: Hair stylist with a steady chair rental and a regular clientele built over eight years.

The relationship ended and the apartment was in the partner's name. The chair rental could not be paid without the housing behind it, and the clients drifted. Names the breakup as the cause of this period of homelessness.
Sleeping in a vehicle for eleven months. This is the first time without housing.
Irregular cash from cutting hair in parking lots and shelters, about $200 a month. No debts on record.

A chronic lung condition. Drinking cost a place on a friend's couch and makes it hard to hold onto any housing. No prescriptions. Keeps clean at a gym. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.
Frequent emergency room visits and police contact over the past six months. Was assaulted after becoming homeless. Trades sex for a place to stay on bad-weather nights. No legal issues.
No children. A network of acquaintances who trade rides and phone charging.

Cuts hair for cash during the day, sleeps in the vehicle, and takes an arrangement for a bed on the worst nights. Does other residents' hair for free on Sundays, which is described as the good part of the week.
A chair in a salon again, and a license renewal that requires a fixed address.
Uses a mobile health van for checkups and has never been referred to housing.
Charismatic and performative, steering toward humor. Becomes flat and factual when describing the exchanges for a bed.

profiles.label: Landscaper with kidney disease
profiles.demographic_line: Age 43. Gender: Male. Race: Black, African American, or African. Location: New York City, New York.
narrative: Restaurant dishwashing and then landscaping for a decade. Left school in the tenth grade.
A back injury ended the landscaping work, the kidney diagnosis followed, the children went into kinship care, and the apartment went with the income. Abuse or trauma did not cause this homelessness.
Sleeping outdoors in an encampment, homeless for four years across six episodes.
No income. Owes a hospital and a former landlord, with a phone bill in collections.

Chronic kidney disease on dialysis, with appointments kept and medication taken. Stimulant use got them removed from a transitional program and makes housing hard to keep. Washes at a drop-in center. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

Repeated emergency room visits in the past six months. Was assaulted during an encampment sweep. No legal issues. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
Three children in kinship care with a relative; visits stopped two years ago. A camp partner who watches belongings.
Wakes early with pain, lines up for a meal, and spends the day at camp watching belongings while the camp partner collects cans. Nothing in the week is described as fulfilling.
Wants dialysis to be manageable and the visits restarted, in that order.
Was enrolled in a transitional program and removed after a positive drug test. Has not reapplied.
Blunt and impatient with paperwork. Quick to anger at questions that sound like judgment, and protective of the camp partner.

profiles.label: Former retail manager, no health issues
profiles.demographic_line: Age 31. Gender: Male. Race: Asian or Asian American. Location: New York City, New York.
narrative: Two years of college on a scholarship lost after a semester away, then five years in retail management.
A family dispute ended with a locked door at nineteen, and again at thirty. Relatives forcing the move-out is what caused this period of homelessness. Abuse or trauma did not cause this homelessness.
Staying in an emergency shelter for eight months. This is the first time without housing.
No income. A defaulted student loan and money owed to people at the shelter.

No health conditions of any kind, no prescriptions, no drinking or drug use. Crowded bathrooms and stolen belongings leave no reliable way to wash, change clothes, or eat regularly. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.
Frequent emergency room visits and police contact over the past six months. Was assaulted at the shelter, has a pending charge, and is being pressured to carry packages for someone there.
Relatives forced the move-out. A younger sibling still texts.
Uses the shelter's computers to job-hunt in the morning, avoids the person applying pressure in the afternoon, and sleeps badly. Nothing in the week is described as fulfilling.
A retail management role, and enough distance from the shelter to stop being asked for favors.
Has filed two incident reports with shelter staff about the pressure, with no result.
Sharp and analytical, describing the situation almost clinically. Frustrated at being read as unwell when the problems are practical.

profiles.label: Night guard with suspended benefits
profiles.demographic_line: Age 68. Gender: Male. Race: Hispanic/Latino/e/a. Location: Cincinnati, Ohio.
narrative: Merchant mariner in youth, then twenty-eight years as a night security guard at the same industrial site.

A change-of-address form was never processed and the Social Security payments stopped. The room was lost within two months, and restoring the benefit now requires an address. No relationship breakdown or family conflict played a part. Abuse or trauma did not cause this homelessness.
Sleeping outdoors, homeless continuously for two years.
No income since the suspension. A hospital bill outstanding.

Congestive heart failure. The prescribed heart medications went untaken once the benefits lapsed. Swelling and fatigue make washing and changing clothes hard. Does not drink or use drugs. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

No emergency room visits or police contact in the past six months, no legal issues, and has not been attacked or threatened. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
No children. A younger relative who has not been located since a move.
Sleeps sitting up because of the swelling, walks to a coffee stand at opening, and spends the day on a bench near the old workplace. Nothing in the week is described as meaningful.
Wants the benefit restored and says nothing about housing beyond that.
An appointment with a benefits advocate has been rescheduled three times.
Quiet and stoic, giving brief answers. Repeatedly says the paperwork 'sorted itself out before', resigned rather than hopeful.

profiles.label: Pipefitter who lost the union card
profiles.demographic_line: Age 49. Gender: Female. Race: Black, African American, or African. Location: Atlanta, Georgia.
narrative: Fifteen years as a union pipefitter with a good rate and steady referrals.

Missed jobs cost the union card, the card cost the income, and the income cost the apartment inside a year. No relationship breakdown or family conflict played a part. Abuse or trauma did not cause this homelessness.
Sleeping outdoors in a camp under a bridge, homeless for five years across seven episodes.
No income. Owes a former landlord and a vehicle repossession balance.

Chronic liver disease. Drinks daily from waking, and the drinking has cost every place they have tried to keep. No prescriptions. Has no consistent way to bathe or wash clothes. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

Frequent emergency room visits over the past six months. Has been assaulted repeatedly at camps. No legal issues. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
Two teenage children living with their other parent. Contact ended four years ago.
Drinks from waking, collects cans in the afternoon, and returns to a camp that has been cleared twice this year. Nothing in the week is described as fulfilling.
Talks about a hearing to get the card reinstated and has never scheduled one.
Detox four times in five years, each following an emergency admission.
Alternates between elaborate plans for getting the card back and long silences. Deeply ashamed of having stopped sending money for the children.

profiles.label: Career musician, benefits intact
profiles.race: American Indian, Alaska Native, or Indigenous
profiles.demographic_line: Age 61. Gender: Female. Race: American Indian, Alaska Native, or Indigenous. Location: Chicago, Illinois.
narrative: Four decades of session and bar work; toured regionally when young and still reads music.

A long decline in bar work, then a hospital admission for the liver, and a landlord who would not renew after the arrears. No relationship breakdown or family conflict played a part. Abuse or trauma did not cause this homelessness.
Staying in an emergency shelter for ten months. This is the first time without housing.
About $980 a month in Social Security, paid on time, plus occasional gig money. No debts.

Cirrhosis. Long-term drinking has cost two apartments. Bipolar disorder, and an episode got them evicted once before. Keeps up with hygiene and does laundry every Thursday. Keeps up with washing, laundry, and meals. No prescriptions.
Frequent emergency room visits and police contact over the past six months. Has been assaulted more than once, has a pending charge, and is being pressured to carry items for someone at the shelter.
A wide circle of musicians who check in. One adult child who visits the shelter monthly.
Plays a weekly set at the drop-in center, keeps to the shelter's schedule, and drinks in the evenings. The weekly set is the highlight of the week.
A single room where an instrument can be kept. Expects it to happen and is not anxious about it.
Sees a psychiatrist at a community clinic and attends most appointments.
Gregarious and rehearsed, offering the same three stories readily. Understates both the drinking and the mental-health history.

profiles.label: Drywall finisher selling medication
profiles.race: American Indian, Alaska Native, or Indigenous
profiles.demographic_line: Age 46. Gender: Female. Race: American Indian, Alaska Native, or Indigenous. Location: Atlanta, Georgia.
narrative: Drywall finishing for two decades, working steadily until a back injury and an opioid prescription.

The injury, the prescription, a switch to street supply, and an eviction inside eighteen months. No relationship breakdown or family conflict played a part. Abuse or trauma did not cause this homelessness.
Sleeping outdoors, homeless for three years across five episodes.
No regular income; sells prescribed medication for cash. Owes a former landlord and a hospital.

COPD. Stimulant use has cost housing more than once. Sells the prescribed pain medication rather than taking it. No reliable way to wash or change clothes. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

Repeated emergency room and crisis-line contact over the past six months. Has been assaulted at camp. No legal issues. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
One adult child who has asked for no contact. A dog that stays at the camp.
Sells what is prescribed at the start of the month, buys what is needed, and spends the rest of the time at the camp with the dog. Nothing in the week is described as fulfilling.
Says the plan is a treatment program later in the year, and gives a different date each time asked.
Has entered three treatment programs and completed none. Currently barred from one shelter.
Polite and evasive, agreeing readily with whatever is suggested and giving inconsistent dates.

profiles.label: Aged out of foster care
profiles.demographic_line: Age 39. Gender: Female. Race: White. Location: Los Angeles, California.
narrative: Grew up in foster care across eleven placements and aged out at 18. Sporadic warehouse and car-wash work since.
Aged out with no placement and has never held a lease. Every stretch of housing since has been someone else's. Does not describe any abuse or trauma as the cause.
Sleeping outdoors, homeless for six years across eight episodes.
No income. Outstanding fines from citations for sleeping in public, and money owed to people who front drugs.

Chronic heart disease. Stimulant use has caused evictions from the few places they have stayed. No prescriptions. No way to keep clean. No mental health condition, head injury, or learning disability.

Constant emergency room and police contact over the past six months. Has been assaulted repeatedly. Has pending charges from the public-sleeping citations, and is being pressured to move packages to clear a debt.
No known family. A partner at the camp, and a long-running conflict with another group.
Moves camp constantly because of the conflict, runs packages to clear the debt, and sleeps in short stretches. Nothing in the week is described as fulfilling.
Wants the debt cleared and the other group to leave them alone. Does not mention housing at all.
Was in the child-welfare system for eleven years and refuses anything that resembles it.
Hypervigilant and fast-talking, testing the interviewer with questions before answering. Unwilling to name who the debts are owed to.

profiles.label: Former EMT after a mass-casualty call
profiles.demographic_line: Age 50. Gender: Male. Race: White. Location: New York City, New York.
narrative: Emergency medical technician for twelve years and a field training officer, until a mass-casualty call. Never returned to work.
Left the service after the call and could not go back, drank through the savings, and the house went. Names the trauma of that call as the cause of this period of homelessness.
Sleeping outdoors, homeless for four years across five episodes.
No income. A disability claim denied twice on appeal, and medical debt in collections.

Cirrhosis. Alcohol dependence that has ended every housing arrangement since. PTSD, diagnosed after the call. The prescribed medications routinely go untaken. Washes at a drop-in center most mornings.

Frequent emergency room visits over the past six months. Was assaulted at a camp. No legal issues. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
Divorced. Two adult children who send money occasionally and do not visit.
Drinks from morning, avoids sirens, and camps far from any road with traffic. Nothing in the week is described as fulfilling.
Says there is no plan and does not expect one.
Two denied disability appeals. Has a lawyer's card and has not called.
Articulate about clinical details and detached about their own case, describing symptoms almost in the third person.

profiles.label: Welder whose relationship broke down
profiles.demographic_line: Age 42. Gender: Male. Race: White. Location: Chicago, Illinois.
narrative: Certified welder with offshore experience and a rate that supported a household.
An offshore injury ended the welding, the relationship broke down during the recovery, and the partner put them out of the shared home. Does not describe it as abuse.
Sleeping outdoors, homeless for seven years across nine episodes.
No income. Restitution owed from an old case and a defaulted car loan.

Chronic pain from the offshore injury limits walking and lifting. Methamphetamine use has cost several places to stay. Schizoaffective disorder, which has led to evictions. No prescriptions. No reliable way to wash or change clothes.

Frequent emergency room visits and police contact over the past six months. Was assaulted after becoming homeless. Has a pending charge that could make renting harder. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money, drugs, or a place to stay.
No contact with family. One friend who holds mail.
Sleeps in daylight where it feels safer, uses at night, and moves before dawn. Nothing in the week is described as fulfilling.
Cannot answer the question and changes the subject each time it is asked.
No follow-up services taken up after several hospital discharges.
Flat affect and long pauses. Describes the breakup only when asked directly, and then in detail.

profiles.label: Kitchen worker, medication supervised
profiles.demographic_line: Age 36. Gender: Female. Race: Black, African American, or African. Location: New York City, New York.
narrative: Left school at 15. A decade of short-term kitchen jobs, never longer than eight months at one place.
Forced out by relatives at nineteen after a family dispute. The pattern since has been eight months of work, a falling-out, and a return to the street. Does not identify abuse or trauma as a cause.
Sleeping outdoors in an encampment, homeless for eight years across ten episodes.
No income. Owes several people at the encampment and has unpaid transit citations.

Chronic asthma. Heroin use has cost every placement. A depressive disorder that has made keeping housing impossible. Takes all medication as prescribed because a drop-in nurse dispenses it in person. No way to meet basic needs like washing and regular meals.
Constant emergency room and police contact over the past six months. Has been assaulted repeatedly, has a pending charge, and is forced to hold and deliver items for others at the camp.
Relatives forced the move-out at 19. Two siblings whose whereabouts are unknown.
Lines up at the drop-in center for the nurse each morning, uses through the day, and returns to the encampment at dusk. Nothing in the week is described as fulfilling.
Answers with whatever the question seems to want, and the answer changes between interviews.
Known to every outreach team in the district and has never held a housing placement.
Guarded and transactional, asking what each answer will get them. Flat and withdrawn when not negotiating.

profiles.label: Former paralegal, cynical about services
profiles.demographic_line: Age 44. Gender: Male. Race: Hispanic/Latino/e/a. Location: Chicago, Illinois.
narrative: Trained as a paralegal and worked eight years in litigation support, with a reputation for thoroughness.

The firm collapsed when the supervising attorney was disbarred. No reference could be obtained, the applications stopped, and the partner they lived with asked them to leave once the income was gone. Nine years have followed. Abuse or trauma did not cause this homelessness.
Sleeping outdoors, moving between three underpasses. Homeless for nine years across twelve episodes.
No income; sells prescribed medication to cover camp debts. Judgments from two creditors.

Emphysema. Alcohol and stimulant use that has ended every housing placement. Bipolar disorder, with episodes that have led to evictions. Sells the prescribed medication rather than taking it. No reliable way to wash or change clothes.
Constant emergency room and police contact over the past six months. Has been assaulted repeatedly, has pending charges, and is made to run errands for a camp lender to work off debts.
One adult child in another state who has blocked contact. The former partner does not answer. No local ties.
Sells the month's prescription in the first week, drinks the rest of the time, and moves between the underpasses. Nothing in the week is described as fulfilling.
Describes the housing system's failures in detail and declines to name anything wanted.
Has been assessed eleven times by six agencies and can quote the score from each.
Precise with dates and documents, openly cynical about services, and swings between rapid, pressured speech and long silences.

profiles.label: Merchant mariner, eleven years outdoors
profiles.race: American Indian, Alaska Native, or Indigenous
profiles.demographic_line: Age 47. Gender: Male. Race: American Indian, Alaska Native, or Indigenous. Location: New York City, New York.
narrative: Merchant mariner from nineteen until a shipboard injury at thirty. No shore trade to fall back on.

A shipboard fire killed a crewmate and left them badly hurt. The injury ended the career, the partner left during the recovery and kept the apartment, and there was no transferable qualification. Names the fire as the cause of this period of homelessness.
Sleeping outdoors under the same underpass, homeless continuously for eleven years. Has not slept indoors in four years.
No income. Debts to hospitals, camp lenders, and a former landlord.

The old back injury limits walking and lifting, and there is a chronic liver condition. Drinks heavily every day, which has ended every short stay indoors. Depression that has led to losing housing. Prescribed medication goes untaken. Cannot keep clean.
Constant emergency room and police contact over the past six months. Has been assaulted repeatedly, has unpaid citations and a pending charge, and is made to hold drugs for a camp lender.
No known living family. A dog that has been a constant for six years.

Wakes with the dog, drinks through the morning, walks a fixed route for bottles and food, and returns to the underpass. Startles at alarms and avoids any open flame. Nothing in the week is described as fulfilling.
Wants somewhere the dog is allowed, and has been told repeatedly that this is not possible.
Offered congregate shelter many times and refuses it because of the dog.
Exhausted and matter-of-fact. Answers every question without hesitation and expects nothing to come of it.

profiles.label: Grocer whose building was sold
profiles.demographic_line: Age 73. Gender: Female. Race: White. Location: Cincinnati, Ohio.
narrative: Ran a neighborhood grocery for thirty years and never worked for anyone else. Knew every customer by name.
The building was sold to a developer and the business closed. A sibling who shared the apartment above the shop took the settlement and put them out. Refuses to describe any of it as abuse or trauma.
Sleeping outdoors, homeless for six years across seven episodes.
Social Security is garnished for an old business debt, leaving almost nothing, and there are further debts to former suppliers.

Heart failure. Drinking that has ended stays with friends. Memory loss and confusion from cognitive decline that have cost housing. Medications go unmanaged and mostly untaken. Cannot keep clean or eat regularly without help.

Frequent emergency room visits and police contact over the past six months. Has been assaulted and robbed at night. Has unpaid citations for selling without a permit and a pending court date. Someone at the corner forces them to hand over the remaining cash each month.
Widowed. One adult child who died, and a grandchild who has not been located. The sibling does not answer.
Sets out goods from a shopping cart on the same corner each morning as though the shop were still open, and is moved along by the afternoon. Nothing in the week is described as fulfilling.
Talks about reopening and gives a date that has already passed.
Refuses the shelter as charity. Accepts a weekly meal from a volunteer van.
Formal and proud, insisting on being addressed by a trade title. Loses track of the question partway through and repeats earlier answers.

profiles.label: Carpenter and union steward
profiles.demographic_line: Age 66. Gender: Male. Race: Black, African American, or African. Location: Atlanta, Georgia.
narrative: Career carpenter and union steward, respected enough to be sent to settle other sites' disputes.

Was beaten on a job site. A long recovery followed, then a foreclosure during it, and the spouse left with what the sale recovered. Names the assault at work as the cause of this period of homelessness.
Sleeping outdoors within the same three blocks, homeless continuously for fourteen years.
No income since benefits lapsed. Debts to hospitals, lenders, and a former landlord.

A head injury, arthritis, and heart disease. Drinks daily, which has ended every placement. Memory loss and disorientation that make keeping housing impossible. Prescribed medications go untaken. Cannot keep clean or change clothes.

Constant emergency room and police contact over the past six months. Has been assaulted at camp, has a warrant for missed court dates, and people at the camp take whatever cash comes in and make them hold drugs.
Estranged from three adult children and the former spouse. No contact with anyone outside the camp.
Cannot give a consistent account of a day beyond drinking. Is found within the same three blocks and does not always recognize the outreach worker. Nothing in the week is described as fulfilling.
Answers with a job that ended in the 1990s.
Assessed many times over fourteen years; the records do not agree with one another.
Disoriented about sequence and dates but vivid about the distant past, and goes quiet at any mention of job sites. Agrees with most questions, which makes verification difficult.

profiles.label: Barista and part-time student
profiles.race: American Indian, Alaska Native, or Indigenous
profiles.demographic_line: Age 26. Gender: Female. Race: American Indian, Alaska Native, or Indigenous. Location: New York City, New York.
narrative: Barista for four years while taking evening classes toward an accounting degree. Halfway through the program.
The building was condemned after an inspection found structural damage, and every tenant had to leave within a week. Not caused by a relationship breakdown, abuse, or trauma.
Staying in an emergency shelter for three weeks. This is the first time without housing.
Works 30 hours a week at the cafe with a steady paycheck. No debts.
No health conditions or disabilities and no prescriptions. Does not use drugs and drinks only occasionally. Keeps up with washing, laundry, and meals. No mental health condition.

No emergency room visits, ambulance rides, hospital stays, crisis calls, or police contact in the past six months. Has not been attacked or threatened since losing housing and has not threatened to harm anyone, including self. No legal issues. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges for money or a place to stay.
Close with two former roommates who meet for dinner every week. No children.
Morning shift at the cafe, an evening class three nights a week, and study time at the library. Says the classes are the best part of the week.
A shared apartment near campus before the next term starts. Has already applied for two.
First stay in any shelter. Has a relocation payment from the city pending.
Calm and practical. Brought a folder with the condemnation notice and pay stubs.

profiles.label: Accountant after a layoff
profiles.demographic_line: Age 58. Gender: Male. Race: Black, African American, or African. Location: New York City, New York.
narrative: Staff accountant at a regional insurance office for twenty-two years.
Laid off in a merger. Severance ran out before a new job came through, and the landlord would not renew a lease without proof of employment. Not caused by a relationship breakdown, abuse, or trauma.
Staying in an emergency shelter for two months. This is the first time without housing.
Receives unemployment benefits every two weeks. No debts.

No chronic health conditions or disabilities. Takes a cholesterol medication as prescribed. Does not use drugs and drinks rarely. Manages washing, laundry, and meals without trouble. No mental health condition.

No emergency room visits, ambulance rides, hospital stays, crisis calls, or police contact in the past six months. Has not been attacked or threatened and has not threatened to harm anyone, including self. No legal issues. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges.
An adult child who calls weekly and two old colleagues who send job leads. No one at home depends on this person.
Applies for jobs every morning at the library, volunteers as a tax-preparation helper two afternoons a week, and walks in the evenings. Enjoys the volunteering.
A bookkeeping job and a one-bedroom apartment. Has a second interview next week.
First stay in any shelter. Working with a job counselor.
Reserved and precise. Embarrassed to be at the shelter but answers every question fully.

profiles.label: Grocery stocker after a building sale
profiles.demographic_line: Age 22. Gender: Female. Race: Asian or Asian American. Location: New York City, New York.
narrative: Finished high school and has stocked shelves at a grocery store for three years.
The landlord sold the house that three roommates rented, and the new owner moved in. Could not find a room fast enough. Not caused by a relationship breakdown, abuse, or trauma.
Living in a transitional housing program for young adults for one month. This is the first time without housing.
Full-time job at the grocery store with a regular paycheck. No debts.
No health conditions or disabilities and no prescriptions. Does not drink or use drugs. Keeps up with washing, laundry, and meals. No mental health condition.

No emergency room visits, ambulance rides, hospital stays, crisis calls, or police contact in the past six months. Has not been attacked or threatened and has not threatened to harm anyone, including self. No legal issues. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges.
Keeps in touch with the old roommates and a cousin nearby. No children.
Day shifts at the store, then pickup basketball at a community center most evenings, which is the favorite part of the day.
A room in a shared apartment within three months, saved for through the program's matched savings plan.
The transitional program helps with budgeting and housing searches.
Easygoing and a little shy; answers briefly but clearly.

profiles.label: Warehouse temp sleeping in a car
profiles.demographic_line: Age 33. Gender: Female. Race: Asian or Asian American. Location: Cincinnati, Ohio.
narrative: Forklift-certified warehouse worker who has taken temp assignments for six years.
A rent increase of $400 a month could not be covered on temp wages. Not caused by a relationship breakdown, abuse, or trauma.
Sleeping in a car in a store parking lot for three months. This is the first time without housing.
Steady temp assignment at a distribution center, paid weekly. No debts.
No health conditions or disabilities and no prescriptions. Does not use drugs and drinks occasionally. Showers at a gym and keeps up with laundry and meals. No mental health condition.

No emergency room visits, ambulance rides, hospital stays, crisis calls, or police contact in the past six months. Has not been attacked or threatened and has not threatened to harm anyone, including self. No legal issues. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges.
Talks with a parent and a best friend every few days. No children.
Day shift at the warehouse, the gym afterward, and a weekend softball league that is the highlight of the week.
An apartment with a lower rent, ideally near the distribution center.
Has not used shelters or services before. Came in to ask about deposit help.
Matter-of-fact and polite. Wants to know how quickly deposit help can come through.

profiles.label: Office cleaner with medical debt
profiles.demographic_line: Age 45. Gender: Female. Race: White. Location: New York City, New York.
narrative: Commercial cleaning supervisor for a building-services company for nine years.
An emergency appendix surgery left a large hospital bill. Paying it down meant falling behind on rent, and the lease was not renewed. Not caused by a relationship breakdown, abuse, or trauma.
Staying in an emergency shelter for five weeks. This is the first time without housing.
Full-time job with a regular paycheck. Owes about $9,000 on the hospital bill and a month of back rent to the former landlord.

Fully recovered from the surgery. No chronic health conditions or disabilities and no prescriptions. Does not drink or use drugs. Keeps up with washing, laundry, and meals. No mental health condition.

No emergency room visits, ambulance rides, hospital stays, crisis calls, or police contact in the past six months. Has not been attacked or threatened and has not threatened to harm anyone, including self. No court cases or fines. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges.
Two close friends from work and a sibling who checks in. No children.
Night shifts supervising a cleaning crew and a weekly community choir rehearsal that is the part of the week most looked forward to.
Set up a payment plan on the hospital bill and rent a studio.
First stay in any shelter. Has an appointment with a financial counselor.
Tired but organized. Brought the hospital bill and pay stubs.

profiles.label: Retired librarian after a rent increase
profiles.demographic_line: Age 67. Gender: Female. Race: Black, African American, or African. Location: Los Angeles, California.
narrative: Public librarian for thirty years before retiring.
The apartment building was renovated and rents nearly doubled. The pension did not stretch to any vacancy found. Not caused by a relationship breakdown, abuse, or trauma.
Staying in an emergency shelter for six weeks. This is the first time without housing.
A monthly pension and Social Security. No debts.
No chronic health conditions or disabilities. Takes a thyroid medication as prescribed. Does not drink or use drugs. Manages washing, laundry, and meals. No mental health condition.

No emergency room visits, ambulance rides, hospital stays, crisis calls, or police contact in the past six months. Has not been attacked or threatened and has not threatened to harm anyone, including self. No legal issues. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges.
Several former coworkers who visit and a former neighbor who helps with apartment listings. No dependents.
Volunteers at a literacy program two mornings a week and reads in the library every afternoon. Describes the tutoring as deeply rewarding.
A unit in a senior apartment building. Is on two waiting lists.
First stay in any shelter. A senior-services caseworker is helping with the waiting lists.
Gracious and articulate. Apologizes for taking up a bed.

profiles.label: Bank teller after a breakup
profiles.demographic_line: Age 30. Gender: Female. Race: Hispanic/Latino/e/a. Location: Cincinnati, Ohio.
narrative: Bank teller for five years, recently promoted to head teller.

A long-term partner ended the relationship and kept the apartment, which was in the partner's name. Lost housing because the relationship broke down. The breakup was not abusive, and abuse or trauma played no part.
Staying in an emergency shelter for one month. This is the first time without housing.
Full-time salary paid twice a month. No debts.
No health conditions or disabilities and no prescriptions. Does not use drugs and drinks socially. Keeps up with washing, laundry, and meals. No mental health condition.

No emergency room visits, ambulance rides, hospital stays, crisis calls, or police contact in the past six months. Has not been attacked or threatened and has not threatened to harm anyone, including self. No legal issues. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges.
Close friends from college and a parent who calls daily. No children.
Works weekdays at the bank, runs with a club on weekends, and enjoys both.
A one-bedroom apartment as soon as first and last month's rent is saved, which should take about six weeks.
Composed and a little embarrassed. Keeps the conversation brief and practical.

profiles.label: Laid-off retail associate on a friend's couch
profiles.race: American Indian, Alaska Native, or Indigenous
profiles.demographic_line: Age 24. Gender: Female. Race: American Indian, Alaska Native, or Indigenous. Location: Chicago, Illinois.
narrative: Retail sales associate since finishing high school.
The store closed and the job went with it. Without income, could not keep up with rent on a shared apartment. Not caused by a relationship breakdown, abuse, or trauma.
Sleeping on a friend's couch for three months. This is the first time without housing.
No income since the store closed. No debts.
No health conditions or disabilities and no prescriptions. Does not use drugs and drinks rarely. Keeps up with washing, laundry, and meals. No mental health condition.

No emergency room visits, ambulance rides, hospital stays, crisis calls, or police contact in the past six months. Has not been attacked or threatened and has not threatened to harm anyone, including self. No legal issues. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and the friend asks for nothing in return.
The friend hosting, a group of high-school friends, and a parent who calls weekly. No children.
Applies for jobs in the morning, plays guitar with friends in the evenings, and takes a free coding class online, which is the most enjoyable part of the week.
Any steady job, then a room of their own.
Has not used shelters or services before.
Friendly and upbeat; a little anxious about overstaying at the friend's place.

profiles.label: Pregnant dental hygienist after a breakup
profiles.demographic_line: Age 27. Gender: Female. Race: White. Location: Cincinnati, Ohio.
narrative: Licensed dental hygienist at a family practice for four years.
Moved out when a relationship ended; the lease was in the partner's name. Lost housing because the relationship broke down. The relationship was not abusive, and abuse or trauma played no part.
Staying in an emergency shelter for three weeks. This is the first time without housing.

Currently pregnant, five months along, with regular prenatal care. No other health conditions or disabilities. Takes prenatal vitamins and no prescription medications. Does not drink or use drugs. Manages washing, laundry, and meals. No mental health condition.

No emergency room visits, ambulance rides, hospital stays, crisis calls, or police contact in the past six months. Has not been attacked or threatened and has not threatened to harm anyone, including self. No legal issues. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges.
Parents live a few hours away and visit often. Friends from work are helping look for apartments.
Works at the dental practice four days a week and goes to a prenatal yoga class that is the favorite part of the week.
A two-bedroom apartment before the baby is due.
First stay in any shelter. A shelter caseworker has referred the case to a family housing program.
Organized and hopeful; asks practical questions about move-in timelines.

profiles.label: Night-shift security guard, repeated stays
profiles.demographic_line: Age 39. Gender: Female. Race: Black, African American, or African. Location: Cincinnati, Ohio.
narrative: Security guard on night shifts for a series of contract companies over ten years.
Contracts end every year or so, and each gap has meant losing a room. Not caused by a relationship breakdown, abuse, or trauma.
Staying in an emergency shelter for two months. This is the fourth time without housing in the past three years.
Current guard contract pays every two weeks. No debts.
No health conditions or disabilities and no prescriptions. Does not use drugs and drinks rarely. Keeps up with washing, laundry, and meals. No mental health condition.

No emergency room visits, ambulance rides, hospital stays, crisis calls, or police contact in the past six months. Has not been attacked or threatened and has not threatened to harm anyone, including self. No legal issues. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges.
Talks with a cousin now and then. No close friends nearby and no children.
Works nights, sleeps in the shelter's day room, and otherwise waits. Has no planned activities and says nothing in the week brings any satisfaction.
A permanent position with one company so the cycle stops.
Knows the shelter staff from the previous three stays.
Quiet and tired; answers in few words.

profiles.label: Retired machinist with lung disease
profiles.race: American Indian, Alaska Native, or Indigenous
profiles.demographic_line: Age 63. Gender: Male. Race: American Indian, Alaska Native, or Indigenous. Location: Los Angeles, California.
narrative: Machinist in a metal-parts shop for thirty-five years.
Retired early when breathing got worse, and the fixed income could not keep up after a rent increase. Not caused by a relationship breakdown, abuse, or trauma.
Staying in an emergency shelter for five weeks. This is the first time without housing.
Social Security and a small pension every month. No debts.
Chronic obstructive lung disease. Uses inhalers exactly as prescribed. Does not drink or use drugs. Manages washing, laundry, and meals, though slowly. No mental health condition.

One clinic visit and no emergency room visits, ambulance rides, hospital stays, crisis calls, or police contact in the past six months. Has not been attacked or threatened and has not threatened to harm anyone, including self. No legal issues. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges.
An adult child in another state who calls weekly and a former coworker who visits. No dependents.
Builds model engines at the shelter's activity table and attends a weekly veterans-and-retirees coffee group. Enjoys both.
First stay in any shelter. A clinic nurse follows the lung condition.
Patient and dry-humored; pauses to catch breath during longer answers.

profiles.label: Line mechanic with a pending charge
profiles.demographic_line: Age 35. Gender: Female. Race: White. Location: Los Angeles, California.
narrative: Auto mechanic at a tire-and-brake shop for eight years.
Spent savings on a lawyer after an arrest for driving on a suspended license, then could not make rent. Not caused by a relationship breakdown, abuse, or trauma.
Staying in an emergency shelter for six weeks. This is the first time without housing.
Still employed full time with a weekly paycheck. Owes $2,500 to the lawyer and $800 in court fees.
No health conditions or disabilities and no prescriptions. Does not use drugs and drinks rarely. Keeps up with washing, laundry, and meals. No mental health condition.

One police contact at the arrest and no emergency room visits, ambulance rides, hospital stays, or crisis calls in the past six months. Has not been attacked or threatened and has not threatened to harm anyone, including self. A pending charge could lead to fines or jail time. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges.
A close friend from the shop and a parent who helps when possible. No children.
Works at the shop all day and restores an old motorcycle with a friend on weekends, which is the best part of the week.
Resolve the case, pay off the lawyer, and rent a studio.
Frank and a little frustrated; owns the mistake and wants to move on.

profiles.label: Painter living in a car for over a year
profiles.demographic_line: Age 50. Gender: Male. Race: Hispanic/Latino/e/a. Location: Atlanta, Georgia.
narrative: House painter, self-employed for most of twenty years.
Work dried up and the landlord would not accept late rent. Not caused by a relationship breakdown, abuse, or trauma.
Sleeping in a car for fourteen months straight. This is the first time without housing.
No regular income; takes occasional cash painting jobs when they come up. No debts.

No health conditions or disabilities and no prescriptions. Does not use drugs and drinks a beer now and then. Keeps up with washing at a community center and with laundry and meals. No mental health condition.

No emergency room visits, ambulance rides, hospital stays, or crisis calls in the past six months, and one conversation with police about parking. Has not been attacked or threatened and has not threatened to harm anyone, including self. No legal issues. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges.
An in-law who offers painting jobs and a couple of old friends. No children.
Looks for painting work in the morning and sketches in a park in the afternoons, which is the most satisfying part of the day.
A small apartment and a steady painting contract.
Has used a car-parking program but no shelters.
Relaxed and talkative; jokes about the car.

profiles.label: Young adult with psychosis off medication
profiles.demographic_line: Age 23. Gender: Male. Race: White. Location: Atlanta, Georgia.
narrative: Finished high school and one semester of community college.
Psychotic symptoms led to arguments with neighbors and an eviction from a supported apartment. Lost housing because of mental health. Not caused by a relationship breakdown, abuse, or trauma.
Staying in an emergency shelter for two months. This is the first time without housing.
Monthly disability benefits, managed with help from a caseworker. No debts.

Diagnosed with schizophrenia. Stopped taking the prescribed antipsychotic two months ago because of side effects. No physical health conditions or disabilities. Does not drink or use drugs. Keeps up with washing, laundry, and meals with reminders from shelter staff.

One clinic appointment and no emergency room visits, ambulance rides, hospital stays, crisis calls, or police contact in the past six months. Has not been attacked or threatened and has not threatened to harm anyone, including self. No legal issues. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges.
A parent who visits on Sundays. No children.
Sits in the shelter day room most of the day. Has no planned activities and does not describe anything as enjoyable.
Unsure; says the parent's house would be fine.
Has a mental health caseworker who visits monthly.
Quiet, with long pauses; sometimes answers a different question than the one asked.

profiles.label: Paralegal who fled an abusive partner
profiles.demographic_line: Age 31. Gender: Male. Race: Black, African American, or African. Location: Atlanta, Georgia.
narrative: Paralegal at a small law firm for six years.
Left the apartment to escape a partner who was physically abusive. Lost housing because of an abusive relationship, and the abuse is the cause of this homelessness.
Staying in an emergency shelter for one month. This is the first time without housing.
Still employed full time with a regular paycheck. No debts.
No chronic health conditions or disabilities and no prescriptions. Does not drink or use drugs. Keeps up with washing, laundry, and meals. No mental health condition.

In the past six months: two emergency room visits for injuries from the partner, one call to a crisis line, and two conversations with police to report the abuse. Has not been attacked or threatened since leaving and has not threatened to harm anyone, including self. No legal issues of their own. Nobody pressures or tricks this person into anything, and there have been no risky exchanges.
A close friend who drives to work some days and a supportive manager. No children.
Works full time and attends a support group twice a week, which is described as the most helpful thing in the week.
A safe apartment at an address the former partner does not know.
A domestic-violence advocate is helping with a protective order.
Composed and careful; asks about how private the records are.

profiles.label: Retired trucker with heart disease in a car
profiles.race: American Indian, Alaska Native, or Indigenous
profiles.demographic_line: Age 61. Gender: Male. Race: American Indian, Alaska Native, or Indigenous. Location: Cincinnati, Ohio.
